name: Shoulder-width training (lateral raises, delts)
lead: Shoulder-width training is a looksmaxxing practice in which people train the deltoid muscles, most often with lateral raises, to make the shoulders look wider. Adding muscle to the sides of the shoulder increases bideltoid width, the measurement across the outer edges of the deltoids, and makes the upper torso look broader relative to the waist. On looksmax.org members post bideltoid measurements, compare them with height and discuss delt work as part of improving frame and proportions [1][2][3].

The deltoid has anterior, intermediate (lateral) and posterior heads, and the intermediate fibres are best positioned to abduct the arm, which is the movement a lateral raise trains [4][10]. Proponents say that developing this muscle adds visible breadth at the top of the torso, and they pair it with the idea of a V-taper, in which wide shoulders contrast with a narrower waist. Practitioners distinguish this soft-tissue width from the bone-based biacromial or clavicle width, which training is said not to change.

Research on the topic is limited. An 8-week 2025 trial in 24 resistance-trained people measured lateral deltoid thickness after dumbbell and cable lateral raises and found increases of roughly 3 to 5 percent [11]. A separate body of attractiveness research examines male body shape, including shoulder dimensions, without testing training programmes [5][7].

paras: The deltoid forms the rounded contour of the shoulder. Its anterior head arises from the clavicle, the intermediate head from the acromion and the posterior head from the spine of the scapula, and all three insert on the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus; the muscle is supplied by the axillary nerve [4]. When all of its fibres contract together it is the prime mover for raising the arm out to the side in the frontal plane; the intermediate fibres do the core abduction work, the anterior fibres assist flexion and the posterior fibres assist extension [4].

In forum usage, "shoulder width" can mean two different things: the bone-based biacromial or clavicle width, and the soft-tissue bideltoid width measured across the outer edges of the deltoids. Training is said to affect the second but not the first. The skeletal side is covered in the article on biacromial and clavicle width.

Wikipedia's article on flies describes the lateral raise (also called the shoulder fly) as an exercise in which the arms rise in the coronal plane to about shoulder height. It works mainly the middle deltoid, with the anterior and posterior heads co-contracting, and the serratus anterior and upper trapezius can take over if the movement is done explosively [10]. It lists common form errors such as swinging the weight with the hips or spine, elbows travelling behind the shoulders and locking out the arms, and notes the article itself carries flags about weak sourcing [10].

The same article describes the inverted (rear delt) fly, performed with the torso parallel to the ground, as mainly working the posterior deltoid, and rowing is described as a transverse extension movement relying on the posterior fibres [10][4]. Posters on looksmax.org describe lateral raises as the staple for the side delt and talk about high-volume or overload variants [2]. A T Nation poster ridicules the number of modified versions of the basic lateral raise, a reminder that the movement is common across lifting communities and not only appearance-focused ones [6].

Threads on looksmax.org include measurement comparisons, for example a user who measured about 20 to 20.5 inches across the shoulders at 6 feet 2 inches and asked whether that was average, with replies giving similar or smaller figures [1]. Other threads ask how to measure bideltoid width, what the minimal width is for a 6 foot 4 inch man to avoid being labelled a "framecel" (a person whose frame is seen as narrow), and invite members to list height and bideltoid width [3][8][9]. In the 6 foot 4 thread, one reply asks whether the poster would stop training shoulders once the target was met [8]. Posters also describe high-volume lateral raise routines as the reason their shoulders look broad [2].
Members commonly pair delt training with the idea of a V-taper. Proponents say clothing and posture can also change how wide the shoulders look.

Bideltoid width is the tape or caliper measurement across the outer deltoids, usually taken at the widest point of the shoulders. A thread on looksmax.org asks how to measure it and another invites members to list their height and bideltoid width [3][9]. "Framecel" is community slang for a person whose frame is seen as narrow, and one thread asks what bideltoid width a 6 foot 4 inch man needs to avoid the label [8].

The V-taper is the visual contrast of wide shoulders and a narrow waist. Members who discuss it say that building the delts and keeping the waist small increases the contrast, and that clothing fit and posture also change how wide the shoulders appear. In the attractiveness literature, Wikipedia's waist-hip ratio article cites a 2005 study reporting that waist-to-chest ratio was the largest determinant of male attractiveness in that work [7].

Muscle growth in the deltoid adds thickness to the sides of the shoulder, so bideltoid measurements can increase with training, while bone-based biacromial or clavicle width is not changed by training [4]. Two 2025 within-participant trials from the same research network examined arm training for muscle thickness: one on lateral raises and one on biceps and triceps work [11][12].

In the lateral raise trial, each of 24 resistance-trained participants did dumbbell raises with one arm and cable raises with the other, twice a week for eight weeks, with five sets to momentary failure per session. Ultrasound measured lateral deltoid thickness, which rose by about 3.3 to 4.6 percent, and the authors report similar growth for the two variants [11]. No trial found measures how much a given gain in bideltoid width changes how the shoulders look to observers.

A 2025 Frontiers in Physiology study (Larsen and colleagues) assigned the arms of 24 resistance-trained men and women to dumbbell or cable lateral raises for eight weeks and measured proximal and distal lateral deltoid thickness by B-mode ultrasound. Thickness increased by about 3.3 to 4.6 percent with no clear difference between the variants [11].

A 2025 International Journal of Exercise Science study (Augustin and colleagues) put 30 young adults through eight weeks of biceps curls and triceps pushdowns, with one arm trained strictly and the other using external momentum. Muscle thickness and arm circumference increases were similar between conditions, while volume load was higher with momentum [12]. This study examined arm muscles and not the deltoid.
No trial has tested shoulder-width training as an appearance intervention. Separate research on male body shape and attractiveness is described under its own heading below [5][7].

Evolutionary and perception research on male body shape has examined shoulder measures. A 2000 Animal Behaviour paper recorded 34 men's voices and took body measures including hip and shoulder width, then compared them with female judgements of the speakers [5]. Wikipedia's waist-hip ratio article cites a 2005 study (Fan et al.) reporting that waist-to-chest ratio was the largest determinant of male attractiveness in that work, with BMI and waist-hip ratio less significant [7]. These studies describe correlations in samples of viewers and do not test whether training changes perceptions.

Wikipedia notes deltoid tears are uncommon and usually follow traumatic shoulder dislocation or large rotator cuff tears, and that the deltoid works with the rotator cuff to stabilise the humeral head under load [4]. Forum replies joke about damaged rotator cuffs from overload sets [2].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, shoulder width is treated as a key frame metric, and lateral raises are the standard answer to the question of how to widen it [1][2].

claims.claim: Lateral raises can make the shoulders visibly broader.
claims.believers: Users post physique updates and attribute broad shoulders to high-volume lateral raises [2].
claims.experts: The deltoid is the prime abductor of the arm, and the lateral raise targets its intermediate fibres [4]. No studies measure appearance outcomes of this training.

claims.claim: Bideltoid size should be compared against height to judge whether the shoulders are narrow.
claims.believers: Members post inches at a stated height and ask whether it is above or below average [1][9].
claims.experts: No published study has examined bideltoid-to-height norms; the attractiveness literature reports ratios such as waist-to-chest instead.[7]

claims.claim: Heavy or very high-volume shoulder work carries injury risk.
claims.believers: Forum replies joke about damaged rotator cuffs from overload sets [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes deltoid tears are uncommon and usually follow dislocation or large rotator cuff tears [4].

claims.claim: Shoulder width beyond a threshold is enough, and training can stop.
claims.believers: Members ask what minimal bideltoid width avoids a narrow-frame label, and some say they would stop training shoulders once they had it [8].
claims.experts: No published threshold exists; attractiveness studies report associations with ratios such as waist-to-chest rather than fixed widths [7].

claims.claim: Dumbbell lateral raises and cable lateral raises build the side delt equally.
claims.believers: Members trade preferences between free-weight and cable versions of the raise, and describe high-volume variants as the key to broad shoulders.[2]
claims.experts: A 2025 within-participant trial of 24 trained lifters found similar lateral deltoid thickness gains from dumbbell and cable raises.[11]

claims.claim: Using momentum (cheating reps) on isolation lifts stops them from building muscle.
claims.believers: Forum posts about overload sets for the lateral delts treat heavy, high-volume work as a route to size.[2]
claims.experts: A 2025 trial found similar arm muscle thickness gains from strict and momentum-assisted curls and pushdowns, with higher volume load under momentum.[12]

angle.text: Training the lateral delts thickens the outer shoulder, so the frame looks wider from the front and the waist looks smaller by contrast. It affects the soft-tissue (bideltoid) width and not the underlying bone width of the clavicles.

card.summary: Building the side delts, mostly with lateral raises, to make the frame look wider; muscle can change visible width but not bone width.
card.aka: delt training, bideltoid width, capped shoulders
card.note: Muscle adds visible shoulder width; skeletal (clavicle) width is not changed by training.

quick.overview:
Shoulder-width training is the looksmaxxing practice of growing the deltoid muscles, especially the side (lateral) heads, so the shoulders look broader. The usual tool is the lateral raise, an arm-abduction exercise.

Community members discuss it as a way to improve upper-body proportions, often alongside the V-taper idea. They also trade bideltoid measurements in inches and compare them to height.
quick.mechanism: The deltoid has three heads that run from the clavicle and shoulder blade to the upper arm, and the middle fibers are best placed to lift the arm out to the side. Growing that muscle adds soft-tissue thickness at the sides of the shoulder, which increases the measured and apparent width. The underlying bone structure stays as it is.
quick.risks: Lifting carries ordinary training risks such as shoulder strain. Forum users joke about rotator cuff damage from very high volume. No studies were found that test shoulder-width training for appearance or attractiveness.
